UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA ALEXANDRIA DIVISION

MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,

Plaintiff,  v.  KATIE HALL, individually; NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN; META PLATFORMS, INC.; and JOHN/JANE DOES 1–6,

Defendants. ____________________________________/

Case No. 1:26-cv-02331

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S RULE 54(b) MOTION TO RECONSIDER ECF NO. 108 AS TO ECF NO. 105

INTRODUCTION

ECF No. 105 requested participation and reporting, not discovery responses. ECF No. 108 denied that request based on postponement of discovery. The Order states: “Here, the record reflects that the District Judge has chosen to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2.

Plaintiff asks the Court to reconsider that application under Rule 54(b). The Court can direct the parties’ planning conference and report and determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after considering the report. Rule 26(a)(1)(C) and Rule 34(b)(2)(A) permit the Court to set a different time for the consequences a conference ordinarily triggers. The Court’s authority under Rules 16 and 26 over the timing and sequence of discovery permits it to make that determination after the parties have conferred. Proposed Order A directs the conference and report and does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. The question on reconsideration is whether postponing the planning steps remains warranted on those terms. If the Court concludes that planning remains postponed, Plaintiff asks that the postponement be stated, its source identified to the extent the Court relies on a direction of the District Judge, and the procedure after the dismissal rulings established. That is Proposed Order B.

Three distinctions govern this Memorandum. First, the denial of the conference request and the explanation for it are different things. The dispute concerns the basis and the continuing effect of the denial, not whether a ruling exists. Second, the Court’s authority to postpone planning and its exercise of that authority are different things. Plaintiff challenges the application of the discretion to the request presented, not the existence of the discretion. Third, an error in the original ruling and a reason to modify it now are different things. The narrowed terms in Proposed Order A support modification now. They do not by themselves prove that ECF No. 108 was erroneous when entered.

I.	ECF NO. 105 REQUESTED PLANNING WITHOUT DISCOVERY RESPONSES

ECF No. 105 asked for an order directing the appearing parties to complete the conference Rule 26(f) requires by a date certain and to file one written report. ECF No. 105 ¶ 11(a)–(b). The report would state the parties’ agreed proposals and each party’s separately attributed position on each subject in Rule 26(f)(3), “including any requested sequencing, phasing, or postponement of discovery and any proposed protective or scheduling terms.” ECF No. 105 ¶ 11(b). The order would not require any party to agree with Plaintiff’s proposals. ECF No. 105 ¶ 6. It would permit each party “to state in the report its position on dismissal, immunity, sequencing, phasing, and any requested postponement of discovery.” Id.

ECF No. 105 stated what it did not seek. It did not request adoption of Plaintiff’s discovery proposals, answers to interrogatories, production of documents, sanctions, or modification of ECF No. 84. ECF No. 105 ¶ 8. The supporting memorandum stated the limit of the request: “This Motion asks the Court to decide when the conference will occur. It does not ask the Court to decide any request concerning the sequencing or postponement of substantive discovery; those requests belong in the report, where each party states its position for the Court’s resolution.” ECF No. 106 at 5. The memorandum recognized the Court’s authority: “The Court retains its authority to modify or defer the process under Rule 26(f)(1) and Rule 16.” Id.

ECF No. 105 also requested an alternative. If the Court postponed the conference, Plaintiff asked that the order identify the scope of the postponement and a definite date or event for renewed consideration. ECF No. 105 ¶ 12; ECF No. 106 at 9.

ECF No. 108 identified that request before denying it. The Order lists the forms of relief sought. It describes the second as “an order directing the parties to complete a Rule 26(f) conference and file respective discovery plans.” ECF No. 108 at 1. It describes the fourth as a request that, if any step is postponed, the order state the date or event on which scheduling will next be addressed. Id. It then denies both motions on the discovery-postponement ground, without prejudice. ECF No. 108 at 2. The Court decided the planning request. This Motion contests the basis of that decision and its operative effect.

The determination Plaintiff requests is this: whether the conference and report should remain postponed when the order directing them does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay, permits any party requesting postponement to state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination, and permits the Court to determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after consideration of the report.

II.	THE RECORD SHOWS A DISAGREEMENT ABOUT PLANNING BEFORE THE DISMISSAL DECISIONS

The chronology supplies four facts that bear on reconsideration.

First, the only stated position of any Defendant is that a conference is premature. Counsel for NCMEC and Hall replied on October 28, 2026: “I believe a Rule 26(f) conference is premature at this juncture, as both Meta and my clients have dispositive motions pending which-- if granted in full-- would be fully dispositive of all claims.” ECF No. 107-3 (Ex. C-1). The reply identified no order or other authority postponing the conference, proposed no date, and did not state whether NCMEC or Hall would oppose an order setting a conference deadline. ECF No. 107 ¶ 8. The reply is attributed to counsel for NCMEC and Hall. It did not state that it was sent on behalf of Meta. Id.

Second, Meta had not responded to the October 16 transmission or the October 28 request as of the execution of Plaintiff’s declaration on October 28, 2026. ECF No. 107 ¶ 9. Plaintiff states Meta’s non-response only as of that date.

Third, the October 30, 2026 response date was requested by Plaintiff. It was not set by the Court. ECF No. 107 ¶ 5; ECF No. 105 ¶ 4. Plaintiff did not contend, and does not contend, that any Defendant defaulted on that date. ECF No. 105 ¶ 4.

Fourth, the conference had not been completed as of the execution of the declaration. ECF No. 107 ¶ 10. Plaintiff’s review of the docket through ECF No. 101 located no order expressly postponing the parties’ Rule 26(f) conference. Id. ECF No. 108 was signed on October 29, 2026, the day after ECF No. 105 was filed and before any Defendant filed a response. The docket therefore contains no statement from any Defendant of its position on an order directing planning on the terms of Proposed Order A.

The chronology explains why Plaintiff sought an order. It does not allege misconduct by any party or counsel, and Plaintiff requests no finding of bad faith.

III.	RECONSIDERATION REQUIRES A SUPPORTED ERROR AND A SUPPORTED CONSEQUENCE

Rule 54(b) provides that an order adjudicating fewer than all the claims or the rights of fewer than all the parties “may be revised at any time before the entry of a judgment adjudicating all the claims and all the parties’ rights and liabilities.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b). The Fourth Circuit has held that “[m]otions for reconsideration of interlocutory orders are not subject to the strict standards applicable to motions for reconsideration of a final judgment.” Am. Canoe Ass’n v. Murphy Farms, Inc., 326 F.3d 505, 514 (4th Cir. 2003). A district court “retains the power to reconsider and modify its interlocutory judgments, including partial summary judgments, at any time prior to final judgment when such is warranted.” Id. at 514–15. That power is committed to the court’s discretion, and the law-of-the-case doctrine guides that discretion. Id. at 515. American Canoe addressed an interlocutory standing determination treated as a partial summary judgment. Id. at 514–16. Plaintiff does not contend that its reasoning imposes a heightened duty here.

The discretion has limits. Rule 54(b) allows more flexibility to revise interlocutory orders before final judgment than Rule 59(e) allows after it, but “the discretion Rule 54(b) provides is not limitless.” Carlson v. Boston Sci. Corp., 856 F.3d 320, 325 (4th Cir. 2017). The Fourth Circuit treats interlocutory rulings as law of the case and permits revision in three circumstances: “(1) a subsequent trial producing substantially different evidence; (2) a change in applicable law; or (3) clear error causing manifest injustice.” Id. (internal quotation marks and alteration omitted). U.S. Tobacco Cooperative applied the same three circumstances and confirmed that the clear-error ground requires more than disagreement with the ruling. U.S. Tobacco Coop. Inc. v. Big S. Wholesale of Va., LLC, 899 F.3d 236, 256–58 (4th Cir. 2018).

Plaintiff invokes the third circumstance. Plaintiff asserts no new evidence and no change in law. A ruling is not clearly erroneous because a different procedure would have been preferable. Plaintiff bears the burden on this Motion. The Order states that Plaintiff “has not established that he is entitled to the relief he seeks.” ECF No. 108 at 1. Plaintiff accepts that burden. Plaintiff must identify an error in the ruling as entered and a consequence that the error works. Plaintiff addresses each separately. Plaintiff then addresses the narrowed terms that support modification now whether or not the Court finds the original error.

A.	The asserted error: the Order treated the conference and report as the commencement of discovery.

ECF No. 108 rests on the postponement of discovery. Its quoted rationale concerns scheduling orders that “initiate discovery obligations” and the avoidance of “expensive or otherwise burdensome discovery on potentially frivolous claims.” ECF No. 108 at 1–2. Its case-specific ground is the District Judge’s choice “to refrain from beginning any discovery until resolution of the pending motions to dismiss.” ECF No. 108 at 2.

ECF No. 105 did not ask the Court to begin discovery. It asked the Court to set the dates for the planning conference and the report. ECF No. 105 ¶ 11(a)–(b). It left every proposal to postpone discovery to the report. ECF No. 105 ¶¶ 6, 11(b); ECF No. 106 at 5. A Defendant that believed no discovery should proceed until the motions were decided could state that position in the report, and the Court would then decide sequencing with each party’s position before it. ECF No. 106 at 5. The request contained the mechanism by which the discovery-postponement decision would be honored.

The Rules separate the conference from discovery. Rule 26(d)(1) places the conference before discovery. Rule 26(a)(1)(C), Rule 26(d)(2)(B), and Rule 34(b)(2)(A) each permit the Court to set a different time for the consequences a conference triggers. The asserted error is that ECF No. 108 applied the discovery-postponement decision as if the conference were the commencement of discovery. The distinction between planning and discovery was presented in ECF No. 105 ¶¶ 6 and 8 and ECF No. 106 at 4–5 and 7–8. Plaintiff does not present it as new. Plaintiff asserts that the Order did not apply it.

ECF No. 108 is an order of this Court. It is not counsel’s assessment of timing, and Plaintiff does not treat it as one. Rule 26(f)(1) permits the Court to order otherwise. Pending dismissal motions do not themselves create an exemption from planning. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 1993 amendment (subdivision (f)). A court may nevertheless direct postponement in the particular action. The question is whether the ground ECF No. 108 states supports postponing planning when the planning order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. On the Order’s own terms, the reason to wait is the burden of discovery. Part V.G addresses that reason as applied to the narrowed procedure.

B.	The asserted consequence: court-directed planning deferred for the pendency of the motions, without implementation terms.

The consequence Plaintiff asserts is limited to what the record supports. When Plaintiff executed the declaration accompanying ECF No. 105, the parties had not completed the conference, and no report containing agreed and competing proposals existed. ECF No. 107 ¶¶ 10–11. The denial defers court-directed planning while three motions to dismiss remain pending. The Order identifies the event that ends the postponement of discovery: resolution of the pending motions to dismiss. ECF No. 108 at 2. It does not state whether the conference and report are postponed with discovery, whether initial disclosures are postponed, what step follows the dismissal rulings, what happens if the rulings issue on different dates, or what happens if a dismissal permits amendment rather than ending the action.

Plaintiff does not assert that evidence has been lost. Plaintiff does not assert an inability to oppose the motions to dismiss. Plaintiff does not assert that the Order prohibits voluntary consultation among the parties. Plaintiff does not assert that procedural uncertainty is, by itself, manifest injustice. The injustice Plaintiff asserts is the postponement of a planning process that the Order’s stated ground did not require to be postponed, for the full pendency of the dismissal motions, if the Court accepts the error stated in Part III.A. If the Court does not accept that error, the implementation terms remain useful, and Proposed Order B supplies them.

C.	The narrowed terms: a reason to modify the Order now.

ECF No. 105 ¶ 11(e)–(f) and ECF No. 106 at 7–9 addressed the relationship between the conference and the Rule 16 schedule and the relationship between the conference and ECF No. 84. They did not make express the terms on the timing of discovery and disclosures that Proposed Order A states. It provides that the order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. It provides that the timing of substantive discovery, initial disclosures, and responses to requests delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order. It provides that nothing in the order decides whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed a discovery stay or modifies any other applicable order. It provides that the Court may determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after consideration of the report. It provides that each Defendant preserves its positions on dismissal, immunity, and the timing of discovery, and states them in the report.

Those terms support modification now. They are not evidence of what ECF No. 105 already requested, and Plaintiff does not present them as such. ECF No. 108 denied ECF No. 105 without prejudice. ECF No. 108 at 2. Plaintiff does not contend that the phrase relaxes the standard for reconsideration. Plaintiff does not read it as an invitation to renew the request before the motions to dismiss are decided. If the Court declines to find error in the original disposition, Plaintiff asks that the Court consider the narrowed terms as a renewed request and decide it on its own merits under Rule 26(f)(1) and Rule 16. Reconsideration remains the principal vehicle. Renewal is a subordinate characterization of the same confined relief.

IV.	RULE 26(f) PERMITS PLANNING WHILE THE COURT CONTROLS DISCOVERY TIMING

A.	The appearing parties share the planning obligation, subject to the Court’s order.

Rule 26(f)(1) provides: “Except in a proceeding exempted from initial disclosure under Rule 26(a)(1)(B) or when the court orders otherwise, the parties must confer as soon as practicable—and in any event at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is to be held or a scheduling order is due under Rule 16(b).” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(1). Rule 26(f)(2) places the obligation jointly on “[t]he attorneys of record and all unrepresented parties that have appeared in the case.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(2). The 1993 Advisory Committee Note states that the obligation “is imposed on all parties that have appeared in the case, including defendants who, because of a pending Rule 12 motion, may not have yet filed an answer in the case.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 1993 amendment (subdivision (f)). Plaintiff relies on the Note for that proposition. Plaintiff does not rely on the Note’s description of deadlines that later amendments replaced.

Two propositions follow. Pending dismissal motions do not themselves exempt a party from planning. The Court may nevertheless postpone planning in a particular action by ordering otherwise. ECF No. 108 is such an order to the extent it postpones the conference. The question on reconsideration is whether that postponement remains warranted when the planning order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay.

B.	The report may present competing proposals, including proposals to defer.

Rule 26(f)(3) requires the discovery plan to state “the parties’ views and proposals” on the timing and form of disclosures; on the subjects and timing of discovery and “whether discovery should be conducted in phases or be limited to or focused on particular issues”; on electronically stored information; on claims of privilege and trial-preparation protection; on changes to the limits on discovery; and on “any other orders that the court should issue under Rule 26(c) or under Rule 16(b) and (c).” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(3)(A)–(F). Rule 26(f)(3)(D), as amended effective December 1, 2025, requires the plan to address “the timing and method for complying with Rule 26(b)(5)(A).” The conference may establish a method for later discovery without requiring immediate production of documents. Plaintiff’s common agenda keys each subject to the provision that requires it. It includes the Rule 26(f)(3)(D) subject. ECF No. 107-1 (Ex. A) § III.

The rule requires good-faith consideration of each subject. It does not require agreement. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(2). The 1993 Note contemplates that the parties may not agree and that the report then indicates their competing proposals. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 1993 amendment (subdivision (f)). A Defendant may propose that no discovery proceed until the motions are decided. That proposal is a view on the subjects Rule 26(f)(3)(B) and (F) identify. The report records it.

Plaintiff does not contend that every planning subject is independent of which claims survive. The scope of preservation, the sources of electronically stored information, and the privilege issues that arise may each depend on the surviving claims. The parties can nevertheless discuss methods and state conditional proposals now, and identify in the report the matters that depend on the dismissal rulings. Proposed Order A requires that engagement. A party may, as to any subject, propose deferral, explain why the subject cannot usefully be resolved before the dismissal rulings, state a conditional proposal, or record a disagreement. Each party must still consider each subject and state its position. A single sentence repeated under every heading is not the participation Rule 26(f)(2) describes.

The 1993 Note also contemplates a report that describes incomplete participation. Id. Plaintiff cannot supply another party’s views. Plaintiff cannot convert an unanswered invitation into that party’s participation. A report describing nonparticipation does not establish that the conference Rule 26(f) requires occurred. Proposed Order A therefore provides for a status report if the conference remains incomplete at the reporting deadline, and provides that a status report does not complete the conference. That provision is a reporting safeguard. It is not an assertion that no other reporting mechanism exists.

C.	Proposed Order A leaves each consequence a conference would otherwise trigger to the Rules and any applicable stipulation or express court order.

Four provisions attach consequences to the Rule 26(f) conference. Proposed Order A addresses each.

Initial disclosures. A party “must make the initial disclosures at or within 14 days after the parties’ Rule 26(f) conference unless a different time is set by stipulation or court order, or unless a party objects during the conference that initial disclosures are not appropriate in this action and states the objection in the proposed discovery plan.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(C). Proposed Order A does not set a different time. The timing of initial disclosures remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order, and any party requesting postponement may state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination. Any objection to disclosures is raised during the conference and stated in the report, as the rule provides.

Discovery sequence. “A party may not seek discovery from any source before the parties have conferred as required by Rule 26(f),” except as the rules, a stipulation, or a court order authorize. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1). The timing of substantive discovery remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order. Proposed Order A does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay, and it does not decide whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed one. It does not restrict informal investigation. It does not displace any order that separately authorizes discovery.

Early document requests. A request under Rule 34 delivered more than 21 days after service “is considered to have been served at the first Rule 26(f) conference.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(2)(B). The responding party must then respond “within 30 days after the parties’ first Rule 26(f) conference,” and “[a] shorter or longer time may be stipulated to under Rule 29 or be ordered by the court.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(A). Local Civil Rule 26(C) prescribes a separate period for serving objections. The record does not establish that any party has delivered a request under Rule 26(d)(2). Proposed Order A addresses the possibility conditionally. It preserves the deemed-service consequence of Rule 26(d)(2)(B), and the time to respond to any such request remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order. It does not declare any request unserved, revive any expired period, or determine any waiver.

Scheduling. Rule 26(f)(1) ties the timing of the conference to the Rule 16(b) schedule. ECF No. 108’s disposition of the scheduling motion, ECF No. 103, is not before the Court on this Motion. Proposed Order A leaves that disposition unchanged. The conference and report it directs are complete in themselves and do not depend on the entry of a scheduling order.

With those provisions, the conference and report require preparation and participation. Proposed Order A does not itself order discovery responses, document production, depositions, or initial disclosures. That is the limited burden the planning order imposes.

D.	Written exchange requires actual engagement.

Rule 26(f)(2) requires the parties to “confer.” The 2000 amendment changed the rule “to require only a ‘conference’ of the parties, rather than a ‘meeting.’” The accompanying Note contemplates other means of conferring, while stating that there are “important benefits to face-to-face discussion,” and the court retains authority to require attendance in person. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 2000 amendment (subdivision (f)); Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(f)(2). The Note does not establish a right to insist on any particular means. Plaintiff does not claim one. Proposed Order A directs substantive written exchange on each subject and permits any other format the participants agree on or the Court directs. Silence does not complete the conference. Transmission of proposals does not complete it. The conference is complete when each participant has stated its position on each subject and the participants have attempted in good faith to agree. ECF No. 107-1 (Ex. A) §§ I, V; ECF No. 106 at 7.

V.	THE ORDER’S DISCOVERY RATIONALE DOES NOT RESOLVE THE MERITS OF THE NARROWED PROCEDURE

Plaintiff addresses the grounds on which the Court or a Defendant may resist the Motion.

A.	The Order’s postponement of planning is the ruling reconsidered, not a ruling denied to exist.

The Order identified the planning request and denied it. ECF No. 108 at 1–2. Plaintiff recognizes that the Order may be read as postponing planning pending the dismissal rulings. Plaintiff does not ask the Court to declare that no ruling on planning exists. Plaintiff asks the Court to reconsider the postponement, on the ground that the reason stated for it concerns the burden of discovery and the narrowed planning order does not itself impose that burden, and in the alternative to state the postponement’s scope and the procedure that follows.

B.	The cost of a report on the narrowed terms is the preparation of positions, not the burden of discovery.

Preparation has a cost. A conference and report require each participant to consider the subjects in Rule 26(f)(3) and state a position. If every claim is dismissed without leave to amend, that work will not be used. The task is limited. The participants are four. Plaintiff’s proposals and agenda already exist. ECF No. 107 ¶¶ 3–4. A Defendant that believes a subject cannot usefully be addressed before the rulings may say so and state a conditional proposal. The report then shows the Court which subjects can be resolved now and which await the rulings. That is the function Rule 26(f)(2) assigns the report. The cost of a report on those terms is the preparation of positions. It is not the cost the Order’s quoted rationale identifies, which is the expense and burden of discovery itself.

C.	The Court can set the timing of each discovery consequence of a conference by order, and Proposed Order A does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay.

A conference triggers discovery consequences absent an order. Rule 26(a)(1)(C) runs disclosures from the conference. Rule 26(d)(1) lifts the bar on seeking discovery once the parties have conferred. Rule 26(d)(2)(B) and Rule 34(b)(2)(A) run the response period for an early-delivered document request from the first conference. Each rule permits the Court to set a different time, and the Court’s authority over the timing and sequence of discovery permits it to determine that timing and sequence after the conference. Proposed Order A does not itself set a different time for any consequence. Any party requesting postponement, phasing, or modification of discovery or disclosure obligations may state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination. Part IV.C states the terms.

D.	The distinction was presented; the narrowed terms were not.

The planning-versus-discovery distinction was argued in ECF No. 105 ¶¶ 6 and 8 and ECF No. 106 at 4–5 and 7–8. Plaintiff does not present it as new evidence. Plaintiff asserts that the Order did not apply it. Plaintiff also presents terms that were not express in ECF No. 105: that the order does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay, that the timing of substantive discovery, initial disclosures, and responses to requests delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order, and that nothing in the order decides whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed a discovery stay. Those terms are a reason to modify the Order now. Plaintiff does not present them as proof that the Order was wrong when entered.

E.	The asserted consequence is stated without enlargement, and the alternative relief does not depend on it.

The consequence Plaintiff asserts is stated in Part III.B. It is the postponement of court-directed planning for the pendency of the motions, without stated implementation terms, when the ground stated for the postponement did not require it. Plaintiff asserts nothing more. If the Court finds that showing insufficient, the alternative relief does not depend on it. A statement of the postponement’s scope and the procedure that follows the dismissal rulings is useful on any view of the original ruling, and ECF No. 105 ¶ 12 requested it.

F.	Relief is requested within whichever source of the postponement operated.

ECF No. 108 attributes the postponement of discovery to a choice by the District Judge. ECF No. 108 at 2. It does not identify the order or instruction that records the choice. Local Civil Rule 72 recognizes that matters may be referred to a magistrate judge on a district judge’s instructions, and such an instruction may not appear as a separately entered order. Plaintiff does not contend that the absence of a docketed order establishes that no instruction exists. Plaintiff does not request internal communications or deliberations. Plaintiff requests identification of the operative direction, to the extent the Court relies on one, so that its scope is known to the parties.

Three possibilities exist. First, a direction of the District Judge may encompass the parties’ conference and the report. If so, Proposed Order B is the appropriate form of relief. It states the postponement, identifies the direction and its scope, and sets the procedure that follows the dismissal rulings. Second, a direction may concern substantive discovery and leave planning available. If so, planning is available for the Court’s consideration under Rule 26(f)(1) on the narrowed terms. Availability does not compel a planning order. Plaintiff asks the Court to exercise its own judgment on those terms. Third, the attribution may reflect an inference from the procedural posture of three pending motions to dismiss and no scheduling order. If so, the Court’s own determination under Rule 26(f)(1) governs, and Plaintiff asks the Court to make it on the narrowed terms.

In no case does Plaintiff ask the Magistrate Judge to countermand a direction of the District Judge. The Motion operates within the authority referred under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(A). Each form of relief requested is consistent with whichever source operated.

G.	The passage the Order quotes concerns the burden of discovery, not an order limited to planning.

ECF No. 108 quotes a decision of another district for the proposition that “Rule 16 Scheduling Orders initiate discovery obligations” and that courts commonly wait for rulings on preliminary motions “to avoid expensive or otherwise burdensome discovery on potentially frivolous claims.” ECF No. 108 at 1–2. Plaintiff addresses that passage as the Order’s stated rationale. Plaintiff does not characterize the holding of the quoted decision, the procedural question it decided, or whether a planning request was before that court. The stated rationale concerns the commencement of discovery and its burden. A planning order that directs a conference and report, and leaves any request for postponement for judicial determination, does not itself initiate discovery obligations. On the Order’s own stated reasoning, the narrowed planning procedure stands outside the reason given for denying ECF No. 105.

VI.	THE PROPOSED ORDERS ADDRESS PLANNING WITHOUT DECIDING DISCOVERY PROPOSALS

A.	Proposed Order A.

Proposed Order A modifies ECF No. 108 as to ECF No. 105 only. The participants are Plaintiff and counsel for NCMEC, Hall, and Meta. The Doe Defendants, unidentified and unserved, are not included. ECF No. 105 ¶ 1. The conference is to be completed within 14 days after entry, by substantive written exchange on the subjects in Rule 26(f)(2)–(3) or by another format the participants agree on or the Court directs. The report is due within 14 days after completion and no later than 18 days after entry. The 14-day period after completion tracks Rule 26(f)(2). The 14-day completion period and the 18-day outer limit are requested terms. To the extent the outer limit requires the report sooner than 14 days after completion, the order shortens the reporting interval under Rule 26(f)(4) and Local Civil Rule 26(A)(1)(b).

The report states agreements as agreements and disagreements as separately attributed positions. Counsel for NCMEC and Hall identifies whether those Defendants adopt a position jointly. ECF No. 107-1 (Ex. A) § V. Plaintiff circulates a proposed report for counsel’s review. The responsibility for the report remains joint under Rule 26(f)(2), and the order adds no interim deadline. If the conference remains incomplete at the reporting deadline, the parties file a status report, or a party unable to obtain a joint report files its own, identifying the participation, the exchanges, and the remaining obstacle. A status report does not complete the conference, extend the completion deadline, or excuse further participation.

Proposed Order A does not independently impose or extend a discovery stay. The timing of substantive discovery, initial disclosures, and responses to requests delivered under Rule 26(d)(2) remains governed by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and any applicable stipulation or express court order. Any party requesting postponement, phasing, or modification of discovery or disclosure obligations may state that position and its grounds in the report for judicial determination. Nothing in the order decides whether ECF No. 108 independently imposed a discovery stay or modifies any other applicable order. The Court may determine the timing and sequence of discovery and disclosures after consideration of the report.
